![Image 1: 
[Much of my site will be useless to you if you've got the images turned off!]
	](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/Images/Utility/empty.gif)

(Vol.IV) Polybius 

 The Histories
----------------------------------

[p429](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/) Fragments of Book XIV
-------------------------------------------------------------------

### [](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/) I.Affairs of Greece

[11a](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/) Perhaps it is true that in all Olympiads the syllabus of events arrests the attention of the reader, owing to their number and importance, the actions of the whole world being brought under one point of view. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)But I think the events of this Olympiad (CXLIV) will have a peculiar power of doing this. For in the first place it was during this Olympiad that the wars in Italy and Africa were brought to an end, wars the final outcome of which who will not be curious to learn? [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For everyone naturally, although he may completely accept our account of particular action and speeches, still always longs to know the end. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Besides this, the political tendencies of the kings were clearly revealed during these years. For all that had been hitherto a matter of gossip about them now became clearly known to everyone, even to those who were not at all disposed to be curious. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For this reason, as I wish to give such an account of the facts as their [p431](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)importance deserves, I have not comprised the events of two years in one Book as was my practice in previous cases.

### [](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/) II.Scipio in Africa

[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The consuls, then, were engaged in these matters, but Publius Scipio, who was in winter quarters in Africa, hearing that the Carthaginians were getting a fleet ready, occupied himself in making his own naval preparations, but continued to prosecute none the less the siege of Utica. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Nor did he entirely abandon his hope of winning over Syphax, but sent frequent messages to him, their armies being at no great distance from each other, feeling sure of indu­cing him to abandon the Carthaginian alliance. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)He thought it indeed not at all unlikely that he had already grown tired of the girl⁠[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/14*.html#note1) for whose sake he had chosen the cause of the Carthaginians, and tired generally of his friendship for Phoenicians, as Scipio well knew the natural tendency of the Numidians to grow disgusted with what pleased them and how lightly they always break their faith to gods and men alike. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)At present his mind was much distracted and agitated by various apprehensions, as he feared an attack owing to the enemy's superiority in numbers, and he gladly availed himself of the following occasion when it offered itself. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Some of his messengers to Syphax reported that the Carthaginians in their winter camp had made their huts from all kinds of wood and branches without any mixture of earth, [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)that the first Numidians to arrive had constructed theirs with [p433](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)reeds, while the others who kept joining the army from the cities had used nothing but branches for the present, some of them being encamped inside but most outside [•](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/secondary/SMIGRA*/Vallum.html)the trench and palisade. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Scipio, therefore, thinking that an attempt to fire the camp would be a complete surprise for the enemy and very serviceable to himself, began to take the necessary measures. [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Syphax in his communications with Scipio always kept harking back to the opinion that the Carthaginians ought to evacuate Italy and the Romans do the same as regards Africa, each nation continuing to occupy the points they held between these two countries. [10](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Scipio had previously refused entirely to listen to this proposal, but he now ordered his messengers to throw out slight hints to the Numidian prince that the attainment of this end was not beyond the bounds of possibility. [11](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Syphax was very much relieved in consequence and became much more disposed than he had been to engage in parleys, [12](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)the consequence being that the messengers became more numerous and their visits more frequent, some of them at times spending several days in the hostile camp without any objection being made. [13](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Scipio on such occasions used to send in the company of his envoys certain expert observers and certain of his officers, looking mean and dirty fellows, disguised as they were in the habit of slaves, with the object of exploring and inspecting undisturbed the approaches and the entrances of both camps. [14](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For there were two of them, one occupied by Hasdrubal with thirty thousand foot and three thousand horse, and another at a distance of [•](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)ten stades belonging to the Numidians and containing about ten thousand horse and fifty thousand foot. [p435](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[15](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The latter was the easiest to attack and the huts very suitable for setting on fire, since the Numidians, as I just said, used neither wood nor earth for their huts, but only reeds and matting.

[2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)As soon as there were signs of the approach of spring, Scipio having now completed all the inquiries necessary for the above design against the enemy, launched his ships and constructed siege-machines to place on them as if he were about to blockade Utica from the sea. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)With his infantry, who numbered about two thousand, he again occupied the hill situated above the town and spared no expense in fortifying this hill and digging a moat round it, giving the enemy the idea that he did so for the purpose of the siege, but in reality desiring to secure himself from possible danger on the day of his enterprise; for he feared lest when his legions had left their camp the garrison of Utica might venture on a sortie, and falling on the camp, which was close by, besiege the force left to defend it. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)While making these preparations he sent a message to Syphax to inquire, on the supposition that the proposed terms met with his own approval, if they would also be agreeable to the Carthaginians and if they could be trusted not to say again that they would further consider before accepting what he was ready to concede. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)He also instructed his envoys not to return to him before receiving an answer to this question. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)When they arrived and Syphax had received the message, he felt convinced that Scipio was determined to conclude the treaty, both because the envoys had told him they would not return without [p437](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)an answer and because of the anxiety shown to make sure of the consent of the Carthaginians. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)So he sent off at once to Hasdrubal informing him of what had occurred and begging him to accept peace, while he himself passed his time at his ease and allowed the Numidians who kept on joining him to encamp outside his fortified camp. [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Scipio pretended to do the same, but as a fact was making every possible preparation for his attack. [10](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)When Syphax had once been instructed by the Carthaginians to conclude the peace, and overjoyed at this, spoke to the envoys on the matter, they at once left for their own camp to tell Scipio the result of the king's action. [11](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The Roman commander, on hearing of it, lost no time in sending other envoys to announce to Syphax that Scipio approved of peace and was earnestly working for it, but that members of the council were of a different opinion, maintaining that matters should rest as they were. [12](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The envoys went to Syphax and informed him to this effect. [13](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Scipio dispatched this embassy in order not to appear to have broken the truce if, while formal negotiations for peace were still in progress, he committed any hostile act. [14](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)But after having made this declaration he considered that whatever happened no one could find fault with his conduct.

[3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Syphax, on hearing this, was no little vexed as he had made up his mind that peace was assured, but he now met Hasdrubal and communicated to him the message he had received from the Romans. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)After much discussion of it they fell to considering [p439](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)how they should now deal with the situation, being very far both in their apprehensions and designs from any suspicion of which was actually about to happen. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For they never had the least thought of taking any precaution for their security or of the likelihood of any disaster, but they were very eager and anxious to take some active steps and to challenge the enemy to battle on level ground. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Scipio, in the meanwhile, by his preparations and the orders he issued gave his soldiery to understand that he was about to make an attempt to seize Utica by surprise, [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)but summoning the ablest and most trusty of his tribunes about midday, and disclosing his plan ordered them to get their supper early and then lead the legions out of the camp, after the trumpeters had all sounded the retreat as usual. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For it is the custom among the Romans at supper-time for the trumpeters and buglers to sound their instruments outside the general's tent as a signal that it is time to set the night-watches at their several stations. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)After this, calling the spies whom he used to send to the enemy's camps, he questioned them closely and compared the accounts they gave of the approaches and entrances of the camps, letting Massanissa decide, and following his advice owing to his personal knowledge of the ground.

[4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)When all was in readiness for his present enterprise, he left a sufficient body of troops suitable for the purpose to guard the camp and advanced with the rest of his army just at the end of the first watch, the enemy being at a distance of sixty stades. [p441](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)When towards the end of the third watch he approached them he placed half of his legionaries and all the Numidians under the command of Gaius Laelius and Massanissa with orders to attack the camp of Syphax, exhorting them to behave like brave men and to do nothing rashly, as they well knew that the more the darkness in night attacks hinders and impedes the sight, the more must one supply the place of actual vision by skill and daring. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)He himself, with the rest of his army, advanced to attack Hasdrubal. He had made up his mind not to deliver his attack before Laelius had set fire to the other hostile camp, and, therefore, this being his purpose, marched at a slow pace. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Laelius and Massanissa dividing their forces into two attacked the enemy simultaneously. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The huts having been, as I stated above, almost specially constructed for the purpose of catching fire, once the front ranks of the Romans had set the fire alight it spread at once over the first row, and made the evil irremediable owing to the closeness of the huts to each other and the quantity of the fuel it fed on. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Laelius remained to cover the operation, and Massanissa, knowing the places by which those who were trying to escape from the flames would have to pass, stationed his own men at those posts. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Absolutely none of the Numidians had any suspicion of the actual fact, not even Syphax, but they all supposed that the camp had caught fire by accident. [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)So that suspecting [p443](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)nothing, some of them aroused from sleep and others surprised while still drinking and carousing, they rushed out of their huts. [10](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Many were trampled to death in the passages that led out of the camp, and many others were caught by the flames and consumed, while all those who escaped from the fire fell into the midst of the enemy and perished without knowing what was happening to them or what they were doing.

[5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Meanwhile the Carthaginians, when they saw the strength of the fire and the volume of flame that rose to the sky, thinking that the Numidian camp had caught fire by accident, rushed some of them to give assistance, while all the rest, flocking out of their camp unarmed, stood in front of it in a state of terror at what was taking place. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Scipio, now that all had gone as well as he could have wished, fell upon those who had come out. Killing some and pursuing others he set their huts also on fire, with the result that the scene of conflagration and general destruction I have just described in the case of the Numidian camp was reproduced in that of the Phoenicians. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Hasdrubal at once entirely desisted from any attempt to extinguish the fire, as he knew now from what had befallen him that the calamity that had befallen the Numidians also was not, as they had supposed, the result of chance but was due to the initiative and daring of the enemy. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)He now thought but of saving himself, and there was very little hope left of even doing this. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For the fire spread with great rapidity, and soon covered the whole area of the camp, the passages of which were full of horses, mules, and men, some half-dead [p445](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)and consumed by the flames, and some frenzied and beside themselves, so that even those ready to make a bold effort were prevented by these obstacles, and owing to the confusion and disturbance there was no hope of safety. [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Syphax, too, and the other officers were in the same plight. The two generals, however, managed to escape with a small body of horse, but of the rest those thousands and thousands of men, horses, and mules met with an unhappy and miserable end in the flames, [11](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)while some of the men trying to escape the fury of the fire died a disgraceful and dishonourable death at the hands of the enemy, cut down as they were naked, not only without their arms but without their clothes. [12](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)In a word the whole place was filled with wailing and confused cries, panic fear, strange noises, and above all raging fire and flames that overbore all resistance, things any one of which would be sufficient to strike terror into a human heart, and how much more this extraordinary combination of them all. [14](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)So it is not possible to find any other disaster which even if exaggerated could be compared with this, so much did it exceed in horror all previous events. [15](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Therefore of all the brilliant exploits performed by Scipio this seems to me the most splendid and most adventurous....

[6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)But when day dawned, and the enemy had all either perished or were in headlong flight, Scipio exhorted his officers and at once started in pursuit. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The Carthaginian commander at first remained where he was, although he had received notice of the approach of the Romans; it was his confidence in the strength of the town in which he was that made him act thus. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)But afterwards, when he saw that [p447](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)the inhabitants of the place were disaffected, the prospect of being attacked by Scipio dismayed him and he continued his flight with all those who had escaped, and who consisted of not less than five hundred horse and about two thousand foot. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Upon this the inhabitants with one accord surrendered at discretion to the Romans. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Scipio spared them, but gave up two of the neighbouring towns to his soldiers to pillage and after this returned to his original camp.

[6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The Carthaginians, now that the prospect of success in their original design had been reversed, were deeply dejected. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For they had hoped to shut in the Romans on the cape adjacent to Utica, which they made their winter quarters, besieging them by land with their armies and by sea with their navy and had made all preparations for this purpose; so that now when by a strange and unexpected disaster they had not only been obliged to abandon to the enemy the command of the open country but expected that at any moment they themselves and their city would be in imminent peril, they became thoroughly dismayed and faint-hearted. [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The situation, however, demanded that they should take precautions and deliberate as to the future, and when the senate assembled it was full of perplexity and the most divergent and tumultuary suggestions abounded. [10](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Some held that they should send to Hannibal and recall him from Italy, their only remaining hope being in that general and his army, [11](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)others proposed sending an embassy to Scipio to ask for a truce and speak to him about terms of peace, while others said they should pluck up courage and [p449](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)communicate with Syphax, [12](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)who had retired to Abba quite near by, and collect the troops who had escaped from the disaster. This was the counsel which finally prevailed.

[13](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The Carthaginians, then, began to assemble their forces, dispatching Hasdrubal to do so, and at the same time sent to Syphax entreating him to help them and to remain firm to his first engagements, assuring him that Hasdrubal would at once join him with his army. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The Roman general both occupied himself with preparations for the siege of Utica and now, on hearing that Syphax remained faithful and that the Carthaginians were again collecting an army, led out his own forces and encamped before that city. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)He also at the same time distributed the booty, but sent about their business the merchants who were making too good an affair of it; for as their recent success had made them form a rosy picture of the future, the soldiers attached no value to their actual booty and were very ready to dispose of it to the merchants for a song.

[4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The Numidian prince and his friends had at first decided to continue their retreat and seek their homes, [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)but when they were met near Abba by the Celtiberians who had been hired by the Carthaginians and who numbered over four thousand, the reliance they placed on this additional force made them halt and pluck up a little courage. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)And when at the same time the young girl, who was, as I have said, the daughter of the general, Hasdrubal, and wife of Syphax, begged and entreated him to remain and not desert the Carthaginians at such a critical [p451](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)time, the Numidian prince suffered himself to be persuaded and yielded to her prayers. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The Celtiberians contributed also not a little to inspire the Carthaginians with hope. For instead of four thousand it was announced that they were ten thousand, and that their personal courage and their armament rendered them invincible in the field. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)These reports and the vulgar gossip of the rabble raised so much the spirits of the Carthaginians that their confidence in being able to take the field once more against the enemy was redoubled. [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Finally in thirty days they encamped and entrenched themselves on the so‑called Great Plain together with the Numidians and Celtiberians, the whole force numbering not less than thirty thousand.

[8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)When the news reached the Roman camp, Scipio at once prepared to advance against them, and after giving the necessary orders to the land and sea forces besieging Utica, he set out on his march, his whole force being in light marching order. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)On the fifth day he reached the Great Plain, and on approaching the enemy encamped for the first day on a hill at a distance of thirty stades from them, [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)but on the next day came down from the hill, and pla­cing his cavalry in front drew up his army at a distance of seven stades from the Carthaginians. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)After remaining where they were for the two subsequent days and making trial of their strength by some slight skirmishing, on the fourth day both generals deliberately advanced their forces and arrayed them for battle. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Scipio simply followed the usual Roman practice of pla­cing the maniples of hastati in front, behind them the principes, and hindmost of all the [p453](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)triarii. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)He stationed his Italian cavalry on his right and the Numidians with Massanissa on the left. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Syphax and Hasdrubal placed the Celtiberians in the centre opposite the Roman maniples, the Numidians on the left, and the Carthaginians on the right. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)At the first encounter the Numidians gave way before the Italian horse and the Carthaginians before Massanissa, their courage having been broken by previous defeats, but the Celtiberians fought bravely holding out against the Romans. [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For they neither had any hope of safety in flight owing to their ignorance of the country, nor could they expect to be spared if made prisoners, owing to their treachery to Scipio in thus coming to fight in the service of Carthage against the Romans in spite of his never having been guilty of any acts of hostility to them during his Spanish campaigns. [11](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)But when the wings gave way they were soon surrounded by the principes and triarii and cut to pieces where they stood except quite a few. [12](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Thus perished the Celtiberians after proving of the greatest service to the Carthaginians not only in the battle but in the flight. [13](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For if the Romans had not met with this obstacle, but had directly pursued the fugitives, very few of the enemy would have escaped. [14](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)But as it was, owing to this stand made by the Celtiberians, Syphax with his cavalry made his way safely back home and Hasdrubal also with the survivors of his force reached Carthage.

p455[9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The Roman general, as soon as he had arranged about the disposal of the booty and prisoners, summoned the council to deliberate as to what should be done next. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)It was decided that Scipio with a part of his army should remain and go round to the several cities, while Laelius and Massanissa with the Numidians and a portion of the Roman legions should follow up Syphax and not give him time to stop and prepare for resistance. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Having come to this decision they separated, these two going after Syphax with the troops I mentioned and the general visiting the towns, some of which surrendered voluntarily to the Romans out of fear, while he besieged and stormed others. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The whole country indeed was inclined for a change, as the people had been constantly exposed to hardship and excessive taxation owing to the long duration of the war in Spain.

[6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)In Carthage itself the disorder had been serious enough previously, but now the city was still more deeply disturbed, and it seemed that after this second heavy blow they had lost all confidence in themselves. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)But nevertheless the advice of those who were thought to be the boldest spirits in the senate was to sail with the fleet against the besiegers of Utica and attempt to raise the siege and engage the enemy's fleet, which was unprepared for an encounter. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)They also demanded that Hannibal should be summoned to return and that resource put to the test without any delay. Both these [p457](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)measures, they said, offered, as far as could be reasonably judged, great chances of saving the country. [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)But others maintained that the time for these steps was past, and that they must now strengthen the city and prepare for a siege. [10](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For if they only preserved concord, chance would afford many opportunities. [11](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)They also advised them to take the question of peace into consideration, and to decide on what terms and by what means they could be delivered from the present evils. [11](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)There were several debates on these proposals and finally they adopted them all. [10](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)As soon as the vote had been taken, those senators who were to sail for Italy proceeded directly from the senate-house to sea, and the admiral went straight on board his ship. The remainder made it their business to see to the defences of the city and met frequently to discuss points of detail.

[2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Scipio's camp was now full of booty, as he met with no resistance but all gave way to him no matter what he attempted, and he decided to send off the great part of the booty to his original camp, and taking with him his army thus lightened to seize on the entrenched position before Tunis and to encamp in full view of Carthage. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For this he thought would be the most effective means of striking the Carthaginians with terror and dismay. The Carthaginians had got ready in a few days the crews and stores for their ships and were about to put to sea to execute their purpose, when Scipio arrived at Tunis and upon its garrison taking to flight occupied the place. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Tunis is situated at a distance of about 120 stades from Carthage, and is visible from nearly the whole town. As I have [p459](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)previously stated, both nature and art have contributed to render it a very strong place. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Just as the Romans had encamped there the Carthaginian fleet was putting to sea on its way to Utica. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Scipio when he saw the enemy under way was much disturbed, as he feared that something untoward might happen to his own fleet, since no one expected to be attacked or had made any preparations for such a contingency. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)He, therefore, at once broke up his camp and marched hastily to the help of his own people. [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Finding that his warships were well provided with facilities for supporting moving forward siege-machines, and in general for all siege operations, but were quite unprepared for a naval action, while the enemy's fleet had during the whole winter been equipping for this very purpose, he abandoned any idea of advancing and offering battle, but anchoring his warships in a line placed round them the transports three or four deep, and then taking down the masts and yards lashed the transports securely to each other with these, leaving a small interval for dispatch-boats to pass in and out.

### [](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/) III.Affairs of Egypt since B.C.213⁠[2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/14*.html#note2)

[11](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Polybius in his fourteenth book says that Philo was the flatterer of Agathocles, the son of Oenanthe and the companion of Ptolemy Philopator....

⁠[3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/14*.html#note3)[2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Polybius in his fourteenth book tells us that there were many portraits in Alexandrian temples of Cleino, the cupbearer of Ptolemy Philadelphus, [p461](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)representing her clothed only in a chiton and holding a rhyton. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)"And are not some of the finest houses," he says, called Myrtion's, Mnesis's, and Potheine's? [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)But what were Mnesis and Potheine but flute-players and Myrtio one of the professional and vulgar mimae? [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)And was not Ptolemy Philopator the slave of the courtesan Agathocleia, who overturned the whole kingdom?"....

[12](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Perhaps some of my readers will wonder why while elsewhere I dealt with the successive events of each year separately, in the case of Egypt alone I give on the present occasion a narrative of occurrences there extending over a considerable period. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The reason of this I may state as follows. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Ptolemy Philopator, of whom I am now talking, after the termination of the war for Coele-Syria abandoned entirely the path of virtue and took to a life of dissipation such as I have just described. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Late in his reign he was forced by circumstances into the war I have mentioned, a war which, apart from the mutual savagery and lawlessness of the combatants, contained nothing worthy of note, no pitched battle, no sea-fight, no siege. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)It, therefore, struck me that my narrative would be easier both for me to write and for my readers to follow if I performed this part of my task not by merely alluding every year to small events not worth serious attention, but by giving once for all a life-like picture so to speak of this king's character.

* * *

(Vol.IV) Polybius 

 The Histories
----------------------------------

[p463](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/) Fragments of Book XV
------------------------------------------------------------------

### [I. Affairs of Italy and Africa](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[º](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)

[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The Carthaginians having captured the Roman transports and a vast quantity of supplies, Scipio was much disturbed, as not only had he been deprived of his own supplies, but the enemy had thus procured for themselves abundance of provisions. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)What aggrieved him still more was that the Carthaginians had violated the late solemn agreement and that the war had thus been rekindled from a fresh source. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)He, therefore, at once appointed as legates Lucius Sergius, Lucius Baebius, and Lucius Fabius, and dispatched them to confer with the Carthaginians about what had occurred and at the same time to inform them that the Roman people had ratified the treaty: [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)for dispatches had just arrived for Scipio informing him of this fact. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)On arriving at Carthage they first of all addressed the senate, and afterwards being brought before the popular assembly, spoke with great freedom about the situation. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)In the first place they reminded the assembly that when the Carthaginian envoys came to Tunis to the Romans and presented themselves before the council, they [p465](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)not only saluted the gods and did obeisance to Earth, as is the custom with other men, [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)but that they debased themselves by falling prostrate on the ground and kissing the feet of the members of the council; and that afterwards when they got up again they accused themselves of having been alone guilty of breaking the original treaty between the Romans and the Carthaginians. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Therefore, they said, they were well justified in any punishment they inflicted on them, but in the name of the common fortune of mankind they had entreated them not to proceed to extremities, but rather let their folly afford a proof of the generosity of the Romans. [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The general himself, they said, and those who had been present then at the council, when they called this to mind, were amazed and asked themselves whence the Carthaginians had the assurance now to ignore what they said on that occasion and to venture on breaking this last solemn treaty. [10](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)It seemed almost evident that they ventured to act thus relying on Hannibal and the forces with him. [11](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)In this confidence they were most ill-advised; for everyone knew quite well, that for the last two years Hannibal and his troops, after abandoning every part of Italy, had fled to the Lacinian promontory, and that, shut in there and almost besieged, they only just succeeded in saving themselves and leaving for Africa. [12](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)"And even," they said, "if they had been coming after a victory in Italy and were about to give battle to us, who have beaten you in two successive battles, your expectation of success should be quite uncertain and you should not only contemplate the prospect of victory but that of a further defeat. [p467](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[13](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)And then what gods will you have to invoke, and on what plea will you be able to supplicate the victors to take pity on your calamity? [14](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Will not your faithlessness and folly exclude you from almost all hope for the mercy of gods and men?"

[2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The ambassadors after making this speech took their departure. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)There were but few among the Carthaginians who approved of adhering to the treaty. The majority both of their leading politicians and of those who took part in the deliberation objected to its harsh conditions, and with difficulty tolerated the bold language of the ambassadors. Besides this, they were not disposed to give up the ships they had brought into port and the supplies they contained. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)But above all they had no slight hopes of conquering with the assistance of Hannibal, but were on the contrary most sanguine. The popular assembly decided simply to dismiss the ambassadors without a reply, [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)but those of the politicians who had determined by any and every means to stir up the war again held a meeting and contrived the following plan. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)They declared that all due care should be taken to ensure the safe arrival of the ambassadors at their own camp and at once prepared two triremes to escort them. Then they sent to the admiral, Hasdrubal, begging him to have some ships ready not far from the Roman camp, so that when the Romans were left by the ships that escorted them they might bear down upon them and sink them. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For the Carthaginian fleet was now anchored off the coast close to Utica. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Having given these instructions to Hasdrubal they [p469](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)sent off the Romans. They had ordered the commanders of the triremes, as soon as they passed the river Macar, to leave the ambassadors in the strait and return, [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)this being a spot from which the enemy's camp could already be seen. [10](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The escort acting on their orders, as soon as they had passed the river-mouth saluted the Romans and sailed back. [11](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Lucius and his colleagues were unsuspicious of any danger but were somewhat put out, thinking it was due to negligence that the escort had left them too soon. [12](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)But as they were continuing their voyage alone three Carthaginian triremes bore down on them as they had been directed to do. When they came up to the Roman quinquereme they could not ram her as she avoided the strokes, nor could they board her as her crew made a gallant resistance. [13](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)But running alongside of her and circling round her they kept on shooting the men on board and killing a number of them, until the Romans, seeing that the men from their own camp who were foraging on the coast were running down to the beach to assist them, managed to run their ship ashore. [15](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Most of the men on board had been killed in the action, but the ambassadors, wonderful to say, escaped.

[3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The consequence of this was that the war began afresh, the cause of its renewal being more serious and more productive of bitter feeling than the original one. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For the Romans, thinking that they had been treacherously attacked, set their hearts on getting the better of the Carthaginians, and the latter, conscious of their guilt, were ready to suffer anything rather than fall into the power of the Romans. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Both sides being animated by such fury, [p471](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)it was evident that the issue must be decided by a battle. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Consequently not only all the inhabitants of Italy and Africa, but those of Spain, Sicily and Sardinia likewise were held in suspense and distracted, awaiting the result.

[5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Hannibal at this time was very poorly off for cavalry and sent to a certain Numidian called Tychaeus, who was a relative of Syphax, and was thought to have the best cavalry in Africa, begging him to help him and join in saving the situation, as he knew well that, if the Carthaginians won, he could retain his principality, but if the Romans were victors, he would risk losing his life too, owing to Massanissa's greed of power. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Accordingly, Tychaeus was prevailed on by this appeal and came to Hannibal with a body of two thousand horse.

[4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Scipio, having taken measures for the security of his fleet, deputed the command to Baebius and himself went round the towns, [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)no longer receiving the submission of those which offered to surrender, but taking them all by assault and selling the inhabitants as slaves, to manifest the anger he felt against the enemy owing to the treacherous behaviour of the Carthaginians. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)He was constantly sending to Massanissa, pointing out to him how the Carthaginians had violated the treaty, and begging him to raise as strong a force as possible and to make haste to join him. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For Massanissa, as I above stated, immediately on the conclusion of the treaty left with his own forces, taking with him besides ten cohorts of Roman cavalry and infantry, and [p473](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)legates on the part of Scipio, in order not only to recover his paternal kingdom, but with the assistance of the Romans to add that of Syphax to it, which he ultimately succeeded in doing.

[5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)It happened that at about the same time the envoys from Rome reached the Roman naval camp. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)So Baebius at once dispatched the Roman envoys to Scipio, but detained the Carthaginians, who were generally dispirited and considered themselves in great danger. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For when they heard of the flagitious treatment of the Roman envoys by the Carthaginians, they thought that vengeance for it would assuredly be taken on themselves. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)But Scipio, on hearing from the Roman legates that both the senate and the people had readily accepted the treaty he had made with the Carthaginians and were ready to comply with all his requests, was highly gratified by this, [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)and ordered Baebius to treat the Carthaginian envoys with all courtesy and send them home, acting, as I think, very rightly and wisely. [10](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For aware as he was of the high value attached by his own nation to keeping faith to ambassadors, he took into consideration not so much the deserts of the Carthaginians as the duty of the Romans. [11](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Therefore restraining his own anger and the bitter resentment he felt owing to the late occurrence, he did his best to preserve "the glorious record of our sires," as the saying is. [12](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The consequence was that he humiliated the people of Carthage and Hannibal himself by thus [p475](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)requiting in ampler measure their baseness by his generosity.

[5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The Carthaginians, when they saw their towns being sacked, sent to Hannibal begging him not to delay, but to approach the enemy and decide matters by a battle. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)After listening to the messengers he bade them in reply pay attention to other matters and be at their ease about this; for he himself would judge when it was time. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)After a few days he shifted his camp from the neighbourhood of Adrumetum and advancing encamped near Zama. This is a town lying five days' journey to the west of Carthage. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)From here he sent out three spies, wishing to find out where the Romans were encamped, and what disposition their general had made in his camp. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)When these men were caught and brought before him Scipio was so far from punishing them, as is the usual practice, that on the contrary he ordered a tribune to attend them and point out clearly the exact arrangement of the camp. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)After this had been done he asked them if the officer had explained everything to them with due diligence. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)When they answered that he had done so, he furnished them with provisions and an escort, and told them to report carefully to Hannibal what had happened to them. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)On their return Hannibal was so much struck with admiration of Scipio's magnanimity and daring, that he conceived, curiously enough, a strong desire to meet him and converse with him. [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Having decided on this he sent a herald saying that he desired to discuss the whole situation with him, [10](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)and Scipio, on receiving the herald's message, [p477](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)assented to the request and said he would send to Hannibal fixing a place and hour for the interview. [11](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Upon this the herald returned to his own camp. [12](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Next day Massanissa arrived with six thousand foot [13](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)and four thousand horse. Scipio received him kindly, congratulating him on having brought under his dominion all the former subjects of Syphax. [14](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)He then broke up his camp and on reaching a town called Naragara encamped there, selecting a spot which was favourably situated in other respects and had water within the throw of a javelin. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)From here he sent to the Carthaginian general saying that he was now ready for the meeting. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)When Hannibal heard this he broke up his camp and on getting within a distance of not more than thirty stades of the Romans encamped on a hill which appeared to be convenient for his present design, but was rather too far away from water, and indeed his men suffered considerable hardship owing to this. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)On the following day both generals came out of their camps accompanied by a few horsemen, and then, leaving their escorts behind, met each other alone, having an interpreter with them. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Hannibal first saluted Scipio and began to speak as follows:

[4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)"Would that neither the Romans had ever coveted any possessions outside Italy, nor the Carthaginians any outside Africa; [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)for both these were very fine empires and empires of which it might be said on the whole that Nature herself had fixed their limits. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)But now that in the first place we went to war with each other for the [p479](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)possession of Sicily and next for that of Spain, now that, finally refusing to listen to the admonition of Fortune, we have gone so far that your native soil was once in imminent danger and our own still is, [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)what remains but to consider by what means we can avert the anger of the gods and compose our present contention? [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)I myself am ready to do so as I learnt by actual experience how fickle Fortune is, and how by a slight turn of the scale either way she brings about changes of the greatest moment, as if she were sporting with little children. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)But I fear that you, Publius, both because you are very young and because success has constantly attended you both in Spain and in Africa, and you have never up to now at least fallen into the counter-current of Fortune, will not be convinced by my words, however worthy of credit they may be. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Consider things by the light of one example, an example not drawn from remote times, but from our own. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)I,then, am that Hannibal who after the battle of Cannae became master of almost the whole of Italy, who not long afterwards advanced even up to Rome, and encamping at forty stades from the walls deliberated with myself how I should treat you and your native soil. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)And now here am I in Africa on the point of negotiating with you, a Roman, for the safety of myself and my country. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Consider this, I beg you, and be not overproud, but take such counsel at the present juncture as a mere man can take, and that is ever to choose the most good and the least evil. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)What man of sense, I ask, would rush into [p481](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)such danger as that which confronts you now? If you conquer you will add but little to the fame of your country and your own, but if you suffer defeat you will utterly efface the memory of all that was grand and glorious in your past. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)What then is the end I would gain by this interview? [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)I propose that all the countries that were formerly a subject of dispute between us, that is Sicily, Sardinia, and Spain, shall belong to Rome and that Carthage shall never make war upon Rome on account of them. Likewise that the other islands lying between Italy and Africa shall belong to Rome. [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Such terms of peace would, I am convinced, be most secure for the Carthaginians and most honourable to you and to all the Romans."

[8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Hannibal having spoken so, Scipio replied. He said that neither for the war about Sicily, nor for that about Spain, were the Romans responsible, [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)but the Carthaginians were evidently the authors of both, as Hannibal himself was well aware. The gods, too, had testified to this by bestowing victory not on the unjust aggressors but on those who had taken up arms to defend themselves. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)No one, he said, was more awake than himself to the fickleness of Fortune and as far as it was in his power he took into consideration the uncertainty of human affairs. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)"But as for the conditions you propose," he continued, "if before the Romans had crossed to Africa you had retired from Italy and then proposed them, I think your expectations would not have been disappointed. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)But now that you have been forced reluctantly to leave Italy, and that we, having crossed into Africa, are in command of the open country, the situation is manifestly much changed. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)And — for this is the most important question — what is the [p483](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)position we have now reached? [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)When your countrymen were beaten and begged for peace we framed a treaty in writing in which it was stipulated, in addition to your present proposals, that Carthaginians should give up their prisoners without ransom, that they should surrender their ships of war, and that they should pay us five thousand talents, and finally that they should give hostages for the performance of those conditions. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)We jointly sent envoys to Rome to submit them to the senate and the people, we Romans stating that we agreed to the terms offered and you Carthaginians entreating that they might be accepted. [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The senate agreed and the people also gave their consent. The Carthaginians, after their request had been granted, most treacherously violated the peace. [11](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)What remains to be done? Put yourself in my place and tell me. Shall we withdraw the most onerous of the conditions imposed? That would be to reward your countrymen for their treachery and teach them to continue to betray their benefactors. [12](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Or shall we grant their present request in the hope of earning their gratitude? But now after obtaining their request by earnest supplication, the moment they conceived the slightest hope from your return, they at once treated us as enemies and foes. [13](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)If we added some conditions even more onerous we might in that case refer the treaty to our popular assembly, but if we withdraw some of the conditions it would be useless even to make mention of this conference at Rome. [14](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Of what further use then is our interview? Either put yourselves and your country at our mercy or fight and conquer us."

p485[9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)After this conversation, which held out no hopes of reconciliation, the two generals parted from each other. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)On the following morning at daybreak they led out their armies and opened the battle, the Carthaginians fighting for their own safety and the dominion of Africa, and the Romans for the empire of the world. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Is there anyone who can remain unmoved in reading the narrative of such an encounter? [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For it would be impossible to find more valiant soldiers, or generals who had been more successful and were more thoroughly exercised in the art of war, nor indeed had Fortune ever offered to contending armies a more splendid prize of victory, since the conquerors would not be masters of Africa and Europe alone, but of all those parts of the world which now hold a place in history; as indeed they very shortly were. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Scipio drew up his army in the following fashion. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)In front he placed the hastati with certain intervals between the maniples and behind them the principes, not pla­cing their maniples, as is the usual Roman custom, opposite to the intervals separating those of the first line, but directly behind these latter at a certain distance owing to the large number of the enemy's elephants. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Last of all he placed the triarii. On his left wing he posted Gaius Laelius with the Italian horse, and on the right wing Massanissa with the whole of his Numidians. [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The intervals of the first maniples he filled up with the cohorts of velites, [p487](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)ordering them to open the action, [10](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)and if they were forced back by the charge of the elephants to retire, those who had time to do so by the straight passages as far as the rear of the whole army, and those who were overtaken to right or left along the intervals between the lines.

[10](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Having made these preparations he rode along the lines and addressed his troops in a few words suitable to the occasion. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)"Bear in mind," he said, "your past battles and fight like brave men worthy of yourselves and your country. Keep it before your eyes that if you overcome your enemies not only will you be unquestioned masters of Africa, but you will gain for yourselves and your country the undisputed command and sovereignty of the rest of the world. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)But if the result of the battle be otherwise, those of you who have fallen bravely in the fight will lie for ever shrouded in the glory of dying thus for their country, [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)while those who save themselves by flight will spend the remainder of their lives in misery and disgrace. For no place in Africa will be able to afford you safety, and if you fall into the hands of the Carthaginians it is plain enough to anyone who gives due thought to it what fate awaits you. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)May none of you, I pray, live to experience that fate. Now that Fortune offers us a choice of the most glorious of prizes, how utterly craven, in short how foolish shall we be, if we reject the greatest of goods and choose the greatest of evils from mere love of life. Go, therefore, to meet the foe with two objects before you, [p489](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)either victory or death. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For men animated by such a spirit must always overcome their adversaries, since they go into battle ready to throw their lives away."

[11](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Such was the substance of Scipio's harangue. Hannibal placed in front of his whole force his elephants, of which he had over eighty, and behind them the mercenaries numbering about twelve thousand. They were composed of Ligurians, Celts, Balearic Islanders, and Moors. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Behind these he placed the native Libyans and Carthaginians, and last of all the troops he had brought over from Italy at a distance of more than a stade from the front lines. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)He secured his wings by cavalry, pla­cing the Numidian allies on the left and the Carthaginian horse on the right. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)He ordered each commanding officer of the mercenaries to address his own men, bidding them be sure of victory as they could rely on his own presence and that of the forces that he had brought back with him. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)As for the Carthaginians, he ordered their commanders to set before their eyes all the sufferings that would befall their wives and children if the result of the battle were adverse. They did as they were ordered, [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)and Hannibal himself went the round of his own troops, begging and imploring them to remember their comrade­ship of seventeen years and the number of the battles they had previously fought against the Romans. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)"In all these battles," he said, "you proved so invincible that you have not left the Romans the smallest hope of ever being able to defeat you. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Above all the rest, and apart from [p491](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)your success in innumerable smaller engagements, keep before your eyes the battle of the Trebia fought against the father of the present Roman general, bear in mind the battle of the Trasimene against Flaminius, and that of Cannae against Aemilius, [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)battles with which the action in which we are about to engage is not worthy of comparison either in respect to the numbers of the forces engaged or the courage of the soldiers." [10](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)He bade them, as he spoke thus, to cast their eyes on the ranks of the enemy. Not only were they fewer, but they were scarcely a fraction of the forces that had formerly faced them, and for courage they were not to be compared with those. [11](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For then their adversaries were men whose strength was unbroken and who had never suffered defeat, but those of to‑day were some of them the children of the former and some the wretched remnant of the legions he had so often vanquished and put to flight in Italy. [12](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Therefore he urged them not to destroy the glorious record of themselves and their general, but, fighting bravely, to confirm their reputation for invincibility.

[13](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Such was the substance of the harangues of the two generals. [12](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)When all was ready for battle on both sides, the Numidian horse having been skirmishing with each other for some time, Hannibal ordered the drivers of the elephants to charge the enemy. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)When the trumpets and bugles sounded shrilly from all sides, some of the animals took fright and at once turned tail and rushed back upon the Numidians who had come up to help the Carthaginians, and Massanissa attacking simultaneously, the Carthaginian left wing was soon left exposed. [p493](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The rest of the elephants falling on the Roman velites in the space between the two main armies, [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)both inflicted and suffered much loss, until finally in their terror some of them escaped through the gaps in the Roman line which Scipio's foresight had provided, so that the Romans suffered no injury, while others fled towards the right and, received by the cavalry with showers of javelins, at length escaped out of the field. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)It was at this moment that Laelius, availing himself of the disturbance created by the elephants, charged the Carthaginian cavalry [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)and forced them to headlong flight. He pressed the pursuit closely, as likewise did Massanissa. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)In the meanwhile both phalanxes slowly and in imposing array advanced on each other, except the troops which Hannibal had brought back from Italy, who remained in their original position. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)When the phalanxes were close to each other, Romans fell upon their foes, raising their war-cry and clashing their shields with their spears as is their practice, [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)while there was a strange confusion of shouts raised by the Carthaginian mercenaries, for, as Homer says, their voice was not one, but

Mixed was the murmur, and confused the sound,

Their names all various,⁠[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/15*.html#note1)

as appears from the list of them I gave above.

[13](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)As the whole battle was a hand-to‑hand affair [the men using neither spears nor swords],⁠[2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/15*.html#note2) the [p495](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)mercenaries at first prevailed by their courage and skill, wounding many of the Romans, [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)but the latter still continued to advance, relying on their admirable order and on the superiority of their arms. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The rear ranks of the Romans followed close on their comrades, cheering them on, but the Carthaginians behaved like cowards, never coming near their mercenaries nor attempting to back them up, [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)so that finally the barbarians gave way, and thinking that they had evidently been left in the lurch by their own side, fell upon those they encountered in their retreat and began to kill them. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)This actually compelled many of the Carthaginians to die like men; for as they were being butchered by their own mercenaries they were obliged against their will to fight both against these and against the Romans, [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)and as when at bay they showed frantic and extraordinary courage, they killed a considerable number both of their mercenaries and of the enemy. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)In this way they even threw the cohorts of the hastati into confusion, but the officers of the principes, seeing what was happening, brought up their ranks to assist, [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)and now the greater number of the Carthaginians and their mercenaries were cut to pieces where they stood, either by themselves or by the hastati. [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Hannibal did not allow the survivors in their flight to mix with his own men but, ordering the foremost ranks to level their spears against them, prevented them from being received into his force. [10](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)They were therefore obliged to retreat towards the wings and the open ground beyond. [14](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The space which separated the two armies still on the field was now covered with blood, slaughter, [p497](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)and dead bodies, and the Roman general was placed in great difficulty by this obstacle to his completing the rout of the enemy. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For he saw that it would be very difficult to pass over the ground without breaking his ranks owing to the quantity of slippery corpses which were still soaked in blood and had fallen in heaps and the number of arms thrown away at haphazard. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)However, after conveying the wounded to the rear and recalling by bugle those of the hastati who were still pursuing the enemy, he stationed the latter in the fore part of the field of battle, opposite the enemy's centre, and making the principes and triarii close up on both wings ordered them to advance over the dead. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)When these troops had surmounted the obstacles and found themselves in a line with the hastati the two phalanxes closed with the greatest eagerness and ardour. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)As they were nearly equal in numbers as well as in spirit and bravery, and were equally well armed, the contest was for long doubtful, the men falling where they stood out of determination, [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)and Massanissa and Laelius, returning from the pursuit of the cavalry, arrived providentially at the proper moment. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)When they fell on Hannibal's army from the rear, most of the men were cut down in their ranks, while of those who took to flight only quite a few escaped, as the cavalry were close on them and the country was level. [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)More than fifteen hundred Romans fell, the Carthaginian loss amounting to twenty thousand killed and nearly the same number of prisoners.

[15](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Such was the result of the final battle between [p499](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Scipio and Hannibal, the battle which decided the war in favour of Rome. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The action over, Scipio after following up the enemy and plundering their camp returned to his own. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Hannibal accompanied by a few horsemen never stopped until he was in safety in Adrumetum. He had done in the battle and before it all that could be done by a good general of long experience. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For, in the first place, he had by his conference with Scipio attempted to terminate the dispute by himself alone; [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)showing thus that while conscious of his former successes he mistrusted Fortune and was fully aware of the part that the unexpected plays in war. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)In the next place, when he offered battle he so managed matters that it was impossible for any commander with the same arms at his disposal to make better dispositions for a contest against the Romans than Hannibal did on that occasion. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The order of a Roman force in battle makes it very difficult to break through, for without any change it enables every man individually and in common with his fellows to present a front in any direction, the maniples which are nearest to the danger turning themselves by a single movement to face it. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Their arms also give the men both protection and confidence owing to the size of the shield and owing to the sword being strong enough to endure repeated blows. So that for these reasons they are formidable antagonists very difficult to overcome. [16](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)But nevertheless to meet each of these advantages Hannibal had shown incomparable skill in adopting at the critical moment all such measures as were in his power and could reasonably be expected to succeed. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For he had hastily collected that large number of elephants and had [p501](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)placed them in front on the day of battle in order to throw the enemy into confusion and break his ranks. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)He had placed the mercenaries in advance with the Carthaginians behind them in order that the Romans before the final engagement might be fatigued by their exertions and that their swords might lose their edge owing to the great slaughter, and also in order to compel the Carthaginians thus hemmed in on both sides to stand fast and fight, in the words of Homer

That e'en the unwilling might be forced to fight.⁠[3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/15*.html#note3)

[4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The most efficient and steadiest of his troops he had placed behind at a certain distance in order that, anticipating and witnessing from afar what took place, they might with undiminished strength and spirit make use of their qualities at the proper time. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)If he, who had never as yet suffered defeat, after taking every possible step to insure victory, yet failed to do so, we must pardon him. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For there are times when Fortune counteracts the plans of valiant men, and again at times, as the proverb says, "A brave man meets another braver yet," as we may say happened in the case of Hannibal.

[17](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)When men give expression to their feelings more violently than is the general custom of their nation, if this excess seems to spring from genuine emotion due to the magnitude of their calamities, it arouses the pity of those who see and hear it, and its very strangeness touches all our hearts; [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)but when such extravagance seems to be a mere piece of charlatanry and acting, it gives rise not to pity but to indignation [p503](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)and disgust. Such was the case on the present occasion with regard to the Carthaginian ambassadors.

[3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Scipio began by stating briefly to them that the Romans were not bound to treat them with leniency for their own sakes, as they confessed that they had begun the war with Rome by taking Saguntum contrary to their treaty and enslaving its inhabitants, and that they had quite recently been guilty of treachery by violating a written agreement they had sworn to observe. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)"But for our own sake," he said, "and in consideration of the fortune of war and of the common condition of man we have decided to be clement and magnanimous. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)This will be evident to you also, if you estimate the situation rightly. For you should not regard it as strange if we impose sufferings and obligations on you or if we demand sacrifices from you, but rather it should surprise you if we grant you any favours, since Fortune owing to your own misconduct has deprived you of any right to pity or pardon and placed you at the mercy of your enemies." [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)After speaking in this sense he informed them first of the indulgences granted to them and afterwards of the severe conditions to which they would have to submit.

[18](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The principal points of the condition proposed were as follows. Carthage was to retain all the cities she formerly possessed in Africa before entering on the last war with Rome, all her former territory, all flocks, herds, slaves, and other property: [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)from that day onward the Carthaginians were to suffer no injury, they were to be governed by their own laws and customs and to receive no garrison. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)These were the lenient conditions; the others of a contrary kind were as follows: Reparation [p505](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)was to be made to the Romans for all acts of injustice committed by the Carthaginians during the truce: prisoners of war and deserters who had fallen into their hands at any date were to be delivered up: they were to surrender their ships of war with the exception of ten triremes, [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)and all their elephants: they were not to make war at all on any nation outside Africa and on no nation in Africa without consulting Rome: [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)they were to restore to King Massanissa, within the boundaries that should subsequently be assigned, all houses, lands, and cities, and other property which had belonged to him or to his ancestors: [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)they were to contribute ten thousand talents in fifty years, paying two hundred Euboic talents each year: [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)finally they were to give as surety a hundred hostages chosen by the Roman general from among their young men between the age of fourteen and thirty.

[19](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)This was the communication that Scipio made to the ambassadors, and after listening to him they lost no time in conveying it to their countrymen in Carthage. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)On this occasion it is said that when one of the senators was about to oppose the acceptance of the terms and was beginning to speak Hannibal came forward and pulled him down from the tribune. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)He, therefore, begged them not to consider whether he had transgressed parliamentary custom, but rather to ask this whether or not he really felt for his country; for this was the sentiment which had now made him guilty of this offence. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)"It seems to me," he said, "astounding and quite incomprehensible, that any man who is a citizen of Carthage and is conscious of the designs that we all individually and as a body have entertained against Rome does not bless his stars that now that he is at the mercy of the Romans he has obtained such lenient terms. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)If you had been asked but a few days ago what you expected your country to suffer in the event of the victory of the Romans, you would not have been able even to give utterance to your fears, so great and excessive were the calamities then in prospect.
