### [](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/) II.Affairs of Macedonia and Greece

#### [](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/) Conduct of Philip and Antiochus regarding Egypt

[20](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)It is very surprising that as long as Ptolemy in his lifetime could dispense with the help of Philip [p509](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)and Antiochus, they were very ready to assist him, [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)but when he died leaving an infant son whom it was their natural duty to maintain in possession of his realm, then encouraging each other they hastened to divide the child's kingdom between themselves and be the ruin of the unhappy orphan. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Nor did they, as tyrants do, take the pains to provide themselves with some paltry pretext for the shameful deed, but at once acted in a fashion so unscrupulous and brutal that they well deserved to have applied to them the saying about the food of fishes, that though they are all of the same tribe the destruction of the smaller ones is food and life to the larger. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Who fancying that he sees reflected in it the image of all impiety towards God and all savagery towards men, as well as of the unbounded covetousness of these two kings? [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)But at the same time who among those who reasonably find fault with Fortune for her conduct of affairs, will not be reconciled to her when he learns how she afterwards made them pay the due penalty, and how she exhibited to their successors as a warning for their edification the exemplary chastisement she inflicted on these princes? [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For even while they were still breaking their faith to each other and tearing to shreds the boy's kingdom she raised up against them the Romans, and very justly and properly visited them with the very evils which they had been contrary to all law designing to bring upon others. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For both of these were very soon vanquished in battle, and they were not only prevented from lusting after the property of others but were compelled to submit and to pay tribute and obey the behests of Rome. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)And, [p511](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)finally, in a very short time Fortune re-established the kingdom of Ptolemy, while as for their dynasties and successors she in one case brought utter destruction upon them and in the other calamities very nearly as grave.

#### [](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/) Philip and the People of Cius

[21](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)There was a certain Molpagoras at Cius, a capable speaker and politician, but in character a demagogue, greedy of power. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)This man, by flattering the populace, by inciting the rabble against men of means, by finally killing some of the latter and banishing others whose property he confiscated and distributed among the people, soon attained by these means to supreme power....

[3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Now the people of Cius met with such disasters not so much owing to chance or to the injustice of their neighbours, but chiefly owing to their own stupidity and misgovernment. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For by advancing ever the worst men to power and punishing those who opposed them in order to plunder the fortunes of their fellow-citizens, [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)they fell as of their own free will into those misfortunes of which we may say that men in general, after being caught in them with their eyes open, not only cannot cure themselves of their folly, but cannot conceive the least suspicion, as even some of the brutes do. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For the latter not only when they have got into trouble themselves from snares and nets, but if they see another animal in danger will not readily approach such engines again, but are even suspicious of the place and mistrust everything they see. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Men on the other hand, though they have heard that some cities have been utterly destroyed by the means I have described, and [p513](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)though they see ruin overtaking others, nevertheless, whenever anyone courts favour with them and holds out to them the hope of repairing their fortunes by laying hands on those of their neighbours, approach the snare without a moment's reflection, though quite aware that of those who have swallowed such baits not a single one has ever been saved, but that measures like the above are well known to have brought destruction on all governments which adopted them....

[22](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Philip having made himself master of the city was highly elated, just as if he had performed a good and noble action in coming readily to the help of his son-in‑law, and overawing the revolutionary party, and then justifiably enriching himself with the prisoners and money he laid hands on. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)He did not see that in the first place the son-in‑law whom he came to help was not wronged, but was wronging others by his treachery, [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)next that by thus without any justification bringing the greatest of calamities on a Hellenic city he would set the seal on the reputation he enjoyed for cruelty to his friends, and that both these crimes would justly leave him a legacy of infamy throughout the whole of Greece as a violator of all that was sacred; [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)thirdly, that he had treated with contumely the ambassadors who came from the cities I mentioned to deliver the Cianians from the perils that menaced them, but who day after day yielding to his entreaties and deluded by him were compelled to be [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)witnesses of things they were far from wishing to see; and finally, that in addition to all he had aroused such savage hate in the Rhodians against [p515](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)him that they would not listen to a word in his favour. [23](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Indeed, chance had very conspicuously intervened to help this matter on. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For just when his envoy was speaking in defence of Philip in the theatre at Rhodes and laying stress on his magnanimity, asserting that, though the city of Cius was now more or less at his mercy, he granted this favour to its people and acted so with the object of confuting the slander of his adversaries and clearly revealing what his true sentiments were; [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)at this very time, I say, a man who had just landed entered the Prytaneum and announced the enslavement of the people of Cius and all Philip's cruelty on that occasion. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)When, therefore, while Philip's ambassador was still speaking the prytanus came forward and communicated the news, the people could not believe it, so black was the treachery. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Philip, therefore, who had rather betrayed himself than the people of Cius, had become so wrong-headed or rather so lost to all sense of decency that he gave himself credit and boasted of conduct of which he should have been most deeply ashamed, as though it were a fine deed. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)From this day forth the Rhodians considered him to be their enemy and made their preparations accordingly, and by this action he made himself equally hated by the Aetolians. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For though he had but recently made his peace with that nation and was extending the hand of fellow­ship to them, now without the shadow of a pretext, at a time when the Aetolians had at no distant date entered into friendship and alliance with Lysimachia, Chalcedon, and Cius, he first of all forced the two former cities to withdraw from this alliance and submit to [p517](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)him, and he now took Cius and enslaved its inhabitants, although an Aetolian strategus was present in the place and at the head of affairs. [10](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Prusias, in so far as his purpose had been accomplished, was gratified, but inasmuch as the prize of the enterprise was carried off by another and he received as his share nothing but the desert site of a city, was much disaffected. He was however, unable to take any action.

#### [](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/) Conduct of Philip

[24](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Philip on his return voyage, committing one act of treachery after another, put in at about midday to Thasos, and though that city was friendly took it and enslaved the inhabitants....

[2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The Thasians told Metrodorus, Philip's general, that they would surrender the city if he would let them remain without a garrison, exempt from tribute, with no soldiers quartered on them and governed by their own laws....

[3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The reply was that Philip acceded to this request upon which all present applauded and admitted Philip into the city....

[4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Perhaps it may be said of all kings that at the beginnings of their reigns they talk of freedom as of a gift they offer to all and style all those who are thus loyal adherents their friends and allies, but as soon as they have established their authority they at once begin to treat those who placed trust in them not as allies but as servants. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Therefore they are disappointed of any credit for noble conduct, though as a rule they do not miss their immediate interest. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)But who would not qualify as perfectly irrational and insane the conduct of a prince, who, engaging [p519](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)in vast enterprises and aspiring to universal dominion, with his chances of success in all his projects still unimpaired, yet in matters of no moment, in the very first matters he was called upon to deal with, proclaimed to all his fickleness and faithlessness?

### [](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/) III.Affairs of Egypt

[24a](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/) As I give a narrative of the successive events that happened in each part of the world in each year, it is evident that in some cases the end must be told before the beginning, in those cases I mean where according to the general scheme of my work and the order imposed on my narrative the locality which was the scene of the final catastrophe occupies an earlier place than that which witnessed the initial stages....

[25](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Sosibius, the pretended guardian of Ptolemy, appears to have been a dexterous instrument of evil who remained long in power and did much mischief in the kingdom. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)He first of all compassed the death of Lysimachus, who was Ptolemy's son by Arsinoë the daughter of Lysimachus, next that of Magas, son of Ptolemy and Berenice, daughter of Magas, thirdly that of Berenice, mother of Ptolemy Philopator, fourthly that of Cleomenes of Sparta, and fifthly that of Arsinoë, the daughter of Berenice.

#### [](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/) Ambition and Fate of Agathocles

[3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)After four or five days, erecting a tribune in the largest colonnade of the palace, they summoned a meeting of the bodyguard and household troops as well as of the officers of the infantry and cavalry. [p521](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)When all these had collected, Agathocles and Sosibius mounted the tribune, and in the first place acknowledged the death of the king and queen and enjoined the populace to go into mourning as was their usual practice. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)After this they crowned the boy and proclaimed him king,⁠[4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/15*.html#note4) and then read a forged will, in which it was written that the king appointed Agathocles and Sosibius guardians of his son. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)They begged the officers to remain well disposed and maintain the boy on his throne; and afterwards brought in two silver urns, the one said to contain the bones of the king and the other those of Arsinoë. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)As a fact, the one did contain the king's bones, but the other was full of spices. Hereupon they at once celebrated the funeral, and now the real circumstances of Arsinoë's fate became manifest to all. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For on her death being made known, everyone began to inquire how she had perished. As there was no other cause assigned when the true report began to reach people's ears, though doubt still subsisted, the truth was impressed on the minds of all, and the people were much stirred in consequence. [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)As for the king, no one cared, but concerning Arsinoë, when some recalled her orphanhood and others the insults and outrages inflicted on her during her whole life, and finally her unhappy death, the people fell into such a state of distraction and affliction that the town was full of groans, tears, and ceaseless lamentation, [10](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)a testimony, in the opinion of those who judged [p523](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)correctly, not so much of affection for Arsinoë as of hatred of Agathocles. [11](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The latter, after depositing the urns in the royal vaults, ordered the public mourning to cease, and as a first step granted two months' pay to the troops, feeling sure of taking the edge off their hatred by appealing to the soldiers' spirit of avarice, and in the next place imposed on them the oath they were accustomed to take on the proclamation of a new king. [12](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)He also sent away Philammon who had carried out the murder of Arsinoë, making him libyarch in the Cyrenaica, and he placed the child in the care of Oenanthe and Agathoclea. [13](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)After this he dispatched Pelops, son of Pelops, to Asia, to King Antiochus to beg him to remain on friendly terms and not to transgress his treaty with the young king's father, and sent Ptolemy, son of Sosibius, to Philip to arrange for the proposed match and to beg for his help if Antiochus attempted any serious violation of his obligations. [14](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)He also appointed Ptolemy, the son of Agesarchus, ambassador to Rome, with the idea not of his hurrying to his post, but of his remaining in Greece when he reached that country and met his friends and relatives there, [15](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)the object of Agathocles being to remove all men of distinction from Egypt. [16](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)He also sent Scopas, the Aetolian, to Greece to hire mercenaries, providing him with a large sum of money to advance to them. [17](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Two reasons underlay this plan; for in the first place, he wished to use the troops he hired for the war against Antiochus, and next to send away the existing force of mercenaries [p525](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)to the country forts in Egypt and to the foreign settlements, and then with these new arrivals to fill up and remodel the household troops and the guards of the court, and of the rest of the city, thinking that the men he himself had enlisted and whom he paid, as they had no political sympathies regarding past events of which they were ignorant, as they reposed their hopes of preservation and advancement on himself, would readily support him and join heartily in executing all his behests. [19](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)All this happened before the negotiations with Philip, as I have stated, but as the negotiations fell to be dealt with first owing to the order of my narrative, it was necessary for me to manage matters so as to give an account of the interviews and speeches of the ambassadors before mentioning their appointment and dispatch.

[20](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Agathocles, as soon as he had removed all the most notable men and checked to a great extent by the advance of pay the disaffection among the troops, turned to his old courses. [21](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)He filled up the vacant places of the royal "friends" by appointing from the body servants and other attendants those most remarkable for their effrontery and recklessness. [22](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)He himself spent the greater part of the day and night in drinking and the debauchery which commonly accompanies it, sparing neither women in the flower of their age nor brides nor virgins, and all this he did with the most odious ostentation. [23](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)So that as strong dislike against him was aroused on all sides, as no attempt was made to conciliate or help those aggrieved, but on the contrary there was a constant repetition of outrage, arrogance, and neglect, [24](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)the [p527](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)former hatred of the populace for him began to fume again, and all recalled the calamities that these men had brought on the kingdom. [25](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)But since they had no leader of any weight, through whom to vent their anger on Agathocles and Agathoclea, they kept quiet, their only remaining hope, to which they eagerly clung, being in Tlepolemus. [26](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)While the king lived, Tlepolemus attended to his own affairs, but on the death of Ptolemy, after quieting the populace, he became again military governor of the district round Pelusium; [27](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)and at first he consulted the king's interest in all he did, believing that there would be some council charged with the guardian­ship of the child and the general control of affairs. [28](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)But when he saw that all the men worthy of this office had been got rid of, and that Agathocles ventured to assume the reins of government, he very soon changed his attitude, as he was conscious of the danger that menaced him owing to their long-standing enmity, and collecting his forces around him took measures for providing himself with money in order that he might not fall an easy prey to any of his foes. [29](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)At the same time he did not despair of himself obtaining the guardian­ship of the child and the direction of affairs, thinking that he was, if his own judgement did not deceive him, more capable because he heard that both the troops under his own command and those in Alexandria placed in him their hopes of overthrowing the insolent domination of Agathocles. [30](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Such being his opinion of himself, the difference between them became [p529](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)speedily more acute, since both of them contributed to this end. [31](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For Tlepolemus, as he was desirous of attaching to himself the commanders, taxiarchs, and inferior officers, entertained them sedulously at banquets; and on those occasions, either flattered by those who wished to make themselves agreeable to him or on his own impulse, since he was young and they were talking over their wine, he would make remarks about the family of Agathocles, at first enigmatical, then of doubtful import, but finally quite outspoken and conveying the most venomous insults. [32](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For he used to toast the wall-dauber and the sackbut-girl and the lady-barber, and the young boy who was so complaisant at the drinking-bouts when he was cupbearer to the king in his childhood's days. [33](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)As his guests always laughed with him and contributed something of their own to his jests, the matter soon reached the ears of Agathocles. [34](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Their enmity was now avowed, and Agathocles lost no time in bringing an accusation against Tlepolemus, charging him with disaffection to the king and stating that he was inviting Antiochus to assume the government. [35](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)He was in no lack of specious grounds for this accusation, some resting on reports of actual facts which he distorted and some being pure inventions of his own. [36](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)All this he did with the object of working up the populace against Tlepolemus, but it had the contrary result. For as they had for long rested their hopes on Tlepolemus, they were exceedingly glad to see the quarrel becoming more inflamed. [37](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The popular movement originated in the following manner. Nicon, [p531](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)who was a relative of Agathocles, had been appointed director of naval affairs during the lifetime of Ptolemy, and he now....

[26a](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/) Agathocles also killed Deinon, son of Deinon, and this was, as the saying is, "the justest of his many iniquities." For at the time when dispatches reached Deinon proposing the murder of Arsinoë, it was perfectly in his power to report the criminal project and save the kingdom, but he chose to take the part of Philammon and became thus the cause of all the evils which followed. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)However, after the murder had been committed, Agathocles found out that he was always recalling his conduct, lamenting it to many people and expressing regret for the chance he had let slip. Therefore he at once met with the punishment he merited and lost his life....

[26](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Agathocles in the first place summoned a meeting of the Macedonians and appeared together with Agathoclea and the young king. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)At first he pretended that he could not say what he wished owing to the abundance of the tears that choked him, but after wiping his eyes many times with his chlamys and subduing the outburst, he took the child in his arms and exclaimed, "Take the child whom his father on his death-bed placed in the arms of this woman," pointing to his sister, "and confided to your faith, you soldiers of Macedon. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)And as to this he told them not to rely on his own word but on that of those who knew the truth and had just come from the very scene of action. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)When the Macedonians heard this, not only did they feel no pity for Agathocles but paid absolutely no attention to his words, and showed such levity by hooting and murmuring to each other that he did not know himself how he got away from the meeting. [10](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Meanwhile numbers of men kept on arriving by boat from the garrisons in upper Egypt, and all begged their relatives or friends to help them at the present crisis and not allow them to be thus outrageously tyrannized over by such unworthy persons. [27](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)There was also one thing done by Agathocles and his party which contributed to exasperate the populace and Tlepolemus. [11](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Nicostratus immediately followed him without saying a word, but striking his thigh with his hand repeatedly. [28](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)It is difficult to describe the strange situation in which Moeragenes found himself. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For some of the executioners stood there with the scourges almost raised to strike him and others were getting the instruments of torture ready before his eyes; [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)but when Nicostratus departed all remained in mute astonishment, looking at each other, and each moment expecting Nicostratus to return; [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)but after a little time had elapsed they gradually dispersed, and Moeragenes was left by himself. After that he was able, much to his surprise, to traverse the palace, and naked as he was rushed into a tent belonging to the Macedonian troops not far from the palace. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Finding them by chance assembled there at breakfast he told his story and the extraordinary manner in which he had been delivered. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)They were disposed to discredit it, but afterwards seeing him naked they were compelled to believe him. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Availing himself of this complete change of circumstances, Moeragenes begged the Macedonians with tears not only to help him to save himself, but to save the king also and chiefly themselves. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)He urged upon them that their destruction was inevitable if they did not avail themselves of the present opportunity, when the hatred of the populace was at its height and everyone was ready to take vengeance on Agathocles. [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)This was just the time, he said, when the feeling was most thoroughly aroused and it only wanted someone to begin. [29](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The Macedonians on hearing this were stimulated to action and finally took the advice of Moeragenes, first without delay visiting the Macedonian tents [p539](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)and then those of the other soldiers, [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)which are all close together, and turned towards a single part of the city. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)As the people had long been disposed to revolt and required only some man of courage to appeal to them, once the movement began it spread like wildfire. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Four hours had scarcely elapsed when men of all nationalities, both soldiers and civilians, had agreed to attack the government. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Chance too co-operated much at this time to the accomplishment of their aim. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For Agathocles, when a letter reached his hands, and some spies were brought before him, and when the letter proved to be the one addressed by Tlepolemus to the troops announcing that he was on the point of coming, and the spies reported that he had actually arrived, [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)so entirely lost his head that, neglecting to take any action or to consider the news he had received, he went to carouse at his usual hour and conducted himself at the banquet in his usual manner. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Oenanthe, who was in great distress, betook herself to the Thesmophoreum, that temple being open for an annual sacrifice. [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)She first of all fell on her knees and with many gestures prayed fervently to the goddesses, and afterwards seated herself by the altar and held her peace. [10](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Most of the women, pleased to see her so dejected and distressed, remained silent, but the relatives of Polycrates and some other noble ladies, who were not yet aware of the danger, came up to her to console her. [11](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)"Come not near me, you beasts," she cried aloud to them, [p541](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)"I know well that you bear us ill-will and that you pray to the goddesses that the worst may befall us, [12](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)but yet I trust that, if it be the will of heaven, I shall yet make you taste the flesh of your own children." [13](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)After saying this she bade her lictors drive them away from her and strike those who refused to leave. [14](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Availing themselves of this pretext all the ladies withdrew, holding up their hands to the goddesses and praying that she might be cursed with the fate that she threatened to bring on others.

[30](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The men had already decided on a revolution, but now that in each house the rage of the women was added to their own, the hatred of the usurper blazed up twice as violent. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)When day again gave place to night, the whole town was full of disturbance and torches and movement. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For some collected in the stadium shouting, some were encouraging each other, others running in different directions took refuge in houses and places not likely to be suspected. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The open spaces round the palace, the stadium, and the great square were now filled with a mixed multitude, including all the crowd of supernumerary performers in the theatre of Dionysus,⁠[5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/15*.html#note5)[5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)and Agathocles, when he heard what was occurring, aroused himself from his drunken slumber, having broken up the banquet a short time previously, and taking all his relatives except Philo went to the king. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)After lamenting his ill-fortune to the boy in a few words he took him by the hand and went up to the gallery between the Maeander and the palaestra leading to the entrance to the theatre. [p543](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)After this, having made fast the first two doors, he retired to the third with a few of the bodyguard, the king, and his own relatives. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The doors were of pen lattice-work and one could see through them, and they were each secured by two bolts. [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Meanwhile the populace were assembling from every part of the city, so that not only level spaces but the roofs and steps were full of people, and there was a confused hubbub and clamour, women and children being mixed with the men. [10](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For in Carthage and also in Alexandria the children play no less a part in such tumults than the men.

[31](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)When the day began to break it was difficult to distinguish the various cries, but that of "Bring the king" predominated. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)At first the Macedonians got up and seized the gate of audience of the palace, [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)but shortly after, when they discovered in what part of the building the king was, they went round and after taking the first door of the gallery off its hinges approached the second and clamoured loudly for the king. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Agathocles was looking now to his own safety and begged the bodyguards to convey a message on his behalf to the Macedonians, stating that he abandoned the office of regent and all his powers and dignities as well as all his revenue, [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)and begged simply for his poor life and a sufficient supply of food, so that retiring into his original obscurity he could not in future, even if he wished it, hurt anyone. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)None of the other bodyguards consented, [p545](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)but Aristomenes alone, who afterwards became minister, undertook this service. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)He was by birth an Acarnanian, and the adulation he had paid to Agathocles in the season of his prosperity was no less conspicuous than his admirable and scrupulous fidelity to the interests of the king and his kingdom when in later life he was at the head of affairs. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For he was the first who having invited Agathocles to dinner presented to him alone among the guests a crown of gold, an honour which is customarily paid only to the king, [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)and he was the first who ventured to wear a ring with Agathocles' portrait engraved on it, and when a daughter was born to him he actually called her Agathoclea. [10](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Perhaps regarding his character I have said enough; but now when he had received Agathocles' commission he went out by a wicket-gate to the Macedonians. [11](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)After he had said a few words to them and explained the proposal, the Macedonians at once attempted to run him through, but when some few persons held their hands over him and begged them to spare him, he went back with orders either to return to them bringing the king or not to come out at all. [12](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Aristomenes, then, was sent back by the Macedonians with this message, and they themselves came up to the second door and broke it in also. [13](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Agathocles and his people, seeing the violence of the Macedonians both by their actions and their determined demand, at first attempted to entreat the soldiers, leaving no word unspoken that might move them to spare their lives at least, Agathocles putting out his hands through the door and Agathoclea her breasts with which she said she had suckled the king. [32](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)When bitterly [p547](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)bewailing their evil fate they found all was useless, they sent out the boy with the bodyguard. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The Macedonians then took the king and at once setting him on a horse conducted him to the stadium. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)His appearance was greeted with loud cheers and clapping of hands, and they now stopped the horse, took him off, and leading him forward placed him in the royal seat. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The joy of the crowd was mingled with regret, for on the one hand they were delighted at having the boy in their hands, but on the other they were displeased that the guilty persons had not been arrested and punished as they deserved. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)So that they continued to shout, demanding that those who had caused all the evil should be taken into custody and made an example. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The day had now advanced, and as the people after all could find no one on whom to vent their resentment, Sosibius, who was the son of Sosibius and at the present time, being a member of the bodyguard, particularly devoted his attention to the king and to affairs of state, [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)seeing that there was no hope of appeasing the fury of the populace and that the boy was ill at ease, finding himself among strangers and amidst all the commotion of the mob, asked the king if he would give up to the people those who were in any way guilty of offences to himself or his mother. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)When the boy nodded his head in assent Sosibius bade some of the bodyguard communicate the royal decision, and making the boy get up led him away to join his household at his own house which was quite near. [19](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)When the king's consent was announced, there was a deafening outburst of cheering and applause all through the stadium. [10](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Meanwhile Agathocles and Agathoclea had separated and each [p549](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)retired to their own residence, and very soon a certain number of soldiers, some on their own initiative and others forced to go by the crowd, set off in search of both.

[33](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The bloodshed and murders which followed were due to the following incident. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Philo, one of Agathocles' attendants and parasites, came out into the stadium suffering from the effects of drink. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)When he observed the popular excitement, he said to those next him, that if Agathocles came out they would have cause to repent again as they had done some days before. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Upon hearing this they began some of them to revile and others to hustle him, and when he attempted to defend himself some very soon tore off his cloak and others levelling their spears at him transpierced him. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Then as soon as he was ignominiously dragged still breathing into the middle of the stadium and the people had tasted blood, they all eagerly waited the arrival of the others. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)It was not long before Agathocles was led in in fetters, and as soon as he entered some people ran up and at once stabbed him, an act of benevolence rather than enmity, for they thus saved him from suffering the fate he deserved. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Next Nicon[º](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/) was brought there and after him Agathoclea stripped naked with her sisters and then all her relatives. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Last of all they dragged Oenanthe from the Thesmophorium and led her to the stadium naked on horseback. [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)All of them were delivered into the hands of the mob, and now some began to bite them with their teeth, some to stab them and others to dig out their eyes. Whenever one of them fell they tore the body from limb to limb until they had thus mutilated them all. [10](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For terrible is the cruelty of the [p551](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Egyptians when their anger is aroused. [11](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)At the same time some young girls who had been Arsinoë's close companions, hearing that Philammon, who had directed the queen's murder, had arrived from Cyrene three days before, rushed to his house and forcing an entrance killed Philammon with clubs and stones; [12](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)strangled his son who was no longer a child, and dragging out his wife naked into the square slew her.

[13](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Such was the end of Agathocles, Agathoclea, and their kindred. [34](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)I am not unaware that some authors in describing these events have introduced the sensational element and worked up their material with the object of making the whole more striking to their readers, largely transgressing the bounds of what is essential to give coherence to their narrative. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Some of them attribute all to Fortune, and lay stress on her instability and on men's incapacity of evading her, while others take count of the strangeness of all that happened, attempting to assign reasons or probable causes to everything. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)It was, however, not my own object to treat these matters in that manner, inasmuch as Agathocles displayed neither courage in war nor conspicuous ability, [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)nor was he fortunate and exemplary in his management of affairs, nor, finally, had he that acuteness and mischievous address which serve a courtier's ends and which made Sosibius and several others so successful until the end of their lives in their management of king after king. On the contrary it was quite different with Agathocles. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Owing to Philopator's incapacity as a ruler he attained an [p553](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)exceptionally high position; [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)and in this position finding himself after that king's death most favourably circumstanced to maintain his power, he lost both his control and his life through his own cowardice and indolence, becoming an object of universal reprobation in quite a short time.

[35](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)It is not therefore advisable, as I said, to deal at excessive length with the fate of such a man, but it is otherwise with the Sicilian Agathocles and Dionysius and certain other rulers of renown. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Of these two, the latter started from an obscure and humble position, and Agathocles, as Timaeus ridiculing him tells us, was a potter and leaving the wheel and the clay and the smoke came to Syracuse as a young man. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)In the first place they both of them became in their time tyrants of Syracuse, a city which then ranked highest in opulence and dignity, [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)and they were afterwards recognized as kings of the whole of Sicily and had made themselves masters even of some parts of Italy. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)And Agathocles not only made an attempt to conquer Africa but retained his exalted position until his death. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)So that they say that Publius Scipio, who was the first to bring Carthage to her knees, when some one asked him whom he thought the greatest statesmen combining courage and wisdom, replied "Agathocles and Dionysius the Sicilians." [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)To the careers of such men indeed it is proper for us to direct the attention of our readers, touching a little on the vicissitudes of fortune and the uncertainty of human affairs, and in general adding to our bare narrative some instructive reflections, but we are by no means called on to do so in the case of the Egyptian Agathocles.

p555[36](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For these reasons I refrained from enlarging on the story of this man, [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)and no less because all sensational occurrences are worthy of attention only when first presented to our view, but afterwards it is not only unprofitable to read about them and keep our eyes on them but such an exercise of our faculties produces a certain disgust. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For since there are two objects, improvement and pleasure, which those who wish to study any subject either by the use of their ears or of their eyes, should keep before them, and since this is especially true of the study of history, a too generous treatment of sensational events contributes to neither. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For not only do abnormal reversals of fortune arouse no emulation, but no one has any permanent pleasure in seeing or reading of things which are contrary to nature and contrary to the general sentiment of mankind. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)It is true we are interested in seeing or hearing of them once for all and at first, just for the sake of observing that what seemed to be impossible is possible, [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)but once we are convinced of this no one takes any pleasure in dwelling on the unnatural, and there is none who would have the least wish to meet with frequent references to the same event of this class. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Therefore what is told us should either excite admiration or cause pleasure, and the elaborate treatment of an event which does neither is suitable rather to tragedy than to history. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Possibly we must excuse writers who do not draw their readers' attention to such matters as are natural or generally happen in the world. [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For they think that among past events the greatest and most wonderful are those which they have met in their personal experience or which particularly arrested their attention when they heard of them [p557](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)from witnesses. [10](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)So that unconsciously they devote too much space to matters which neither are novel, others having spoken of them before, nor are able to benefit or to please us. I have now said enough on this subject.

### [](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/) IV.Affairs of Asia

#### [](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/) Character of Antiochus

[37](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)King Antiochus seems to have been at first a man who both conceived great projects and possessed courage and the capability of executing his designs, [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)but as he advanced in life he showed himself much inferior to his former self and disappointed general expectation.

2.description: Battle of Zama, victory (202 BCE) of the Romans led by Scipio Africanus the Elder over the Carthaginians commanded by Hannibal. The last and decisive battle of the Second Punic War, it effectively ended both Hannibal’s command of Carthaginian forces and also Carthage’s chances to significantly oppose Rome.

**Battle of Zama**, (202 bce), victory of the Romans led by [Scipio Africanus the Elder](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Scipio-Africanus) over the Carthaginians commanded by [Hannibal](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Hannibal-Carthaginian-general-247-183-BCE). The last and [decisive](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/decisive) battle of the [Second Punic War](https://www.britannica.com/event/Second-Punic-War), it effectively ended both Hannibal’s command of Carthaginian forces and also [Carthage](https://www.britannica.com/place/Carthage-ancient-city-Tunisia)’s chances to significantly oppose [Rome](https://www.britannica.com/place/ancient-Rome). The battle took place at a site identified by the Roman historian [Livy](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Livy) as Naraggara (now Sāqiyat Sīdī Yūsuf, [Tunisia](https://www.britannica.com/place/Tunisia)). The name Zama was given to the site (which modern historians have never precisely identified) by the Roman historian [Cornelius Nepos](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Cornelius-Nepos) about 150 years after the battle.

By the year 203 [Carthage](https://www.britannica.com/place/Carthage-ancient-city-Tunisia) was in great danger of attack from the forces of the Roman general [Publius Cornelius Scipio](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Publius-Cornelius-Scipio), who had invaded Africa and had won an important battle barely 20 miles (32 km) west of Carthage itself. The Carthaginian generals Hannibal and his brother [Mago](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Mago-Carthaginian-general) were accordingly recalled from their campaigns in Italy. Hannibal returned to Africa with his 12,000-man veteran army and soon gathered a total of 37,000 troops with which to defend the approaches to Carthage. Mago, who had [sustained](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/sustained) battle wounds during a losing engagement in [Liguria](https://www.britannica.com/place/Liguria) (near [Genoa](https://www.britannica.com/place/Genoa-Italy)), died at sea during the crossing.

Scipio, for his part, marched up the Bagradas ([Majardah](https://www.britannica.com/place/Wadi-Majardah)) River toward Carthage, seeking a decisive battle with the Carthaginians. Some of Scipio’s Roman forces were reinvigorated veterans from [Cannae](https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Cannae) who sought redemption from that disgraceful defeat. Once his allies had arrived, Scipio had about the same number of troops as Hannibal (around 40,000 men), but his 6,100 cavalrymen, led by the [Numidian](https://www.britannica.com/place/Numidia) ruler [Masinissa](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Masinissa) and the Roman general [Gaius Laelius](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Gaius-Laelius), were superior to the Carthaginian cavalry in both training and quantity. Because Hannibal could not transport the majority of his horses from Italy, he was forced to [slaughter](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/slaughter) them to keep them from falling into Roman hands. Thus, he could field only about 4,000 [cavalry](https://www.britannica.com/topic/cavalry), the bulk of them from a minor [Numidian](https://www.britannica.com/place/Numidia) ally named Tychaeus.

Hannibal arrived too late to prevent Masinissa from joining up with Scipio, leaving Scipio in a position to choose the battle site. That was a reversal of the situation in Italy, where Hannibal had held the advantage in cavalry and had typically chosen the ground. In addition to utilizing 80 war [elephants](https://www.britannica.com/animal/elephant-mammal) that were not fully trained, Hannibal was also compelled to rely mostly upon an army of Carthaginian recruits that lacked much battle experience. Of his three battle lines, only his seasoned veterans from Italy (between 12,000 to 15,000 men) were accustomed to fighting Romans; they were positioned at the rear of his formation.

Before the battle, Hannibal and Scipio met personally, possibly because Hannibal, perceiving that battle conditions did not favour him, hoped to negotiate a generous settlement. Scipio may have been curious to meet Hannibal, but he refused the proposed terms, stating that Carthage had broken the truce and would have to face the [consequences](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/consequences). According to Livy, Hannibal told Scipio, “What I was years ago at [Trasimene](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Battle-of-Trasimene) and [Cannae](https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Cannae), you are today.” Scipio is said to have replied with a message for Carthage: “Prepare to fight because evidently you have found peace intolerable.” The next day was set for battle.

As the two armies approached each other, the Carthaginians unloosed their 80 elephants into the ranks of the Roman [infantry](https://www.britannica.com/topic/infantry), but the great beasts were soon dispersed and their threat neutralized. The failure of the elephant charge can likely be explained by a trio of factors, with the first two being well documented and most important. First, the elephants were not well trained. Second—and perhaps even more vital to the outcome—Scipio had arranged his forces in maniples (small, flexible infantry units) with broad alleys between them. He had trained his men to move to the side when the elephants charged, locking their shields and facing the alleys as the elephants passed by. That caused the elephants to run unimpeded through the lines with little, if any, engagement. Third, the loud shouts and blaring trumpets of the Romans may have disconcerted the elephants, some of which swerved to the side early in the battle and instead attacked their own infantry, causing [chaos](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/chaos) on the front line of Hannibal’s recruits.

Scipio’s cavalry then charged the opposing Carthaginian cavalry on the wings; the latter fled and were pursued by Masinissa’s forces. The Roman infantry legions then advanced and attacked Hannibal’s infantry, which consisted of three consecutive lines of defense. The Romans crushed the soldiers of the first line and then those of the second. However, by that time the legionnaires had become nearly exhausted—and they had yet to close with the third line, which consisted of Hannibal’s veterans from his Italian campaign (i.e., his best troops). At that crucial juncture, Masinissa’s Numidian cavalry returned from their [rout](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/rout) of the enemy cavalry and attacked the rear of the Carthaginian infantry, who were soon crushed between the combined Roman infantry and the cavalry assault. Some 20,000 Carthaginians died in the battle, and perhaps 20,000 were captured, while the Romans lost about 1,500 dead. The Greek historian [Polybius](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Polybius) states that Hannibal had done all that he could as a general in battle, especially considering the advantage held by his opponent. That Hannibal was fighting from a position of weakness does not in any way diminish Scipio’s victory for Rome, however. With the defeat of Carthage and Hannibal, it is likely that Zama awakened in Rome a vision of a larger future for itself in the [Mediterranean](https://www.britannica.com/place/Mediterranean-Sea).

The Battle of Zama left Carthage helpless, and the city accepted Scipio’s peace terms whereby it [ceded](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/ceded) Spain to Rome, surrendered most of its warships, and began paying a 50-year indemnity to Rome. Scipio was awarded the surname Africanus in tribute of his victory. Hannibal escaped from the battle and went to his estates in the east near [Hadrumetum](https://www.britannica.com/place/Hadrumetum) for some time before he returned to Carthage. For the first time in decades, Hannibal was without a military command, and never again did he lead Carthaginians into battle. The indemnity Rome set as payment from Carthage was 10,000 silver talents, more than three times the size of the indemnity demanded at the conclusion of the [First Punic War](https://www.britannica.com/event/First-Punic-War). Although the Carthaginians had to publicly burn at least 100 ships, Scipio did not [impose](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/impose) harsh terms on Hannibal himself, and Hannibal was soon elected as suffete (civil magistrate) by popular vote to help administer a defeated Carthage.

**Second Punic War**, second (218–201 bce) in a series of wars between the [Roman Republic](https://www.britannica.com/place/Roman-Republic) and the Carthaginian (Punic) empire that resulted in Roman [hegemony](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/hegemony) over the western Mediterranean.

In the years after the [First Punic War](https://www.britannica.com/event/First-Punic-War), Rome wrested Corsica and [Sardinia](https://www.britannica.com/place/Sardinia-island-Italy) from [Carthage](https://www.britannica.com/place/Carthage-ancient-city-Tunisia) and forced Carthaginians to pay an even greater indemnity than the payment exacted immediately following the [war](https://www.britannica.com/topic/war). Eventually, however, under the leadership of [Hamilcar Barca](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Hamilcar-Barca), his son [Hannibal](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Hannibal-Carthaginian-general-247-183-BCE), and his son-in-law Hasdrubal, Carthage acquired a new base in [Spain](https://www.britannica.com/topic/history-of-Spain), whence they could renew the war against Rome.

In 219 Hannibal captured Saguntum (Sagunto) on the east coast of the [Iberian Peninsula](https://www.britannica.com/place/Iberian-Peninsula). Rome demanded his withdrawal, but Carthage refused to recall him, and Rome declared war. Because Rome controlled the sea, Hannibal led his army overland through Spain and [Gaul](https://www.britannica.com/place/Gaul-ancient-region-Europe) and across the Alps, arriving in the plain of the Po River valley in 218 bce with 20,000 [infantry](https://www.britannica.com/topic/infantry) and 6,000 [cavalry](https://www.britannica.com/topic/cavalry). Roman troops tried to bar his advance but were outmatched, and Hannibal’s hold over northern Italy was established. In 217 Hannibal, reinforced by Gallic tribesmen, marched south. Rather than attack Rome directly, he marched on [Capua](https://www.britannica.com/place/Capua-ancient-city-Italy), the second largest town in Italy, hoping to incite the populace to rebel. He won several battles but still refrained from attacking the city of Rome, even after [annihilating](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/annihilating) a huge Roman army at Cannae in 216. The defeat [galvanized](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/galvanized) Roman resistance. A brilliant defensive strategy conducted by Quintus Fabius Maximus [Cunctator](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Quintus-Fabius-Maximus-Verrucosus) harried the Carthaginians without offering battle. Thus, the two armies remained deadlocked on the Italian peninsula until 211 bce, when Rome recaptured the city of [Capua](https://www.britannica.com/place/Capua-Italy).

In 207 [Hasdrubal](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Hasdrubal-Carthaginian-general-died-207-BCE), following Hannibal’s route across the Alps, reached northern Italy with another large army supported by legions of Ligurians and Gauls. Hasdrubal marched down the peninsula to join Hannibal for an assault on Rome. Rome, exhausted by war, nevertheless raised and dispatched an army to check Hasdrubal. [Gaius Nero](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Gaius-Claudius-Nero), commander of the southern Roman army, slipped away north also and defeated Hasdrubal on the banks of the Metauros River. Hannibal maintained his position in southern Italy until 203, when he was ordered to return to Africa. Italy was free of enemy troops for the first time in 15 years. During the long mainland campaign, fighting had continued as well on Sardinia and [Sicily](https://www.britannica.com/place/Sicily), which had become Rome’s chief sources of food. Aided by internal upheaval in [Syracuse](https://www.britannica.com/place/Syracuse-Italy), Carthage reestablished its presence on the island in 215 and maintained it until 210. Meanwhile, in Spain, Roman forces maintained pressure on Carthaginian strongholds. The Roman general [Publius Scipio](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Scipio-Africanus) won a decisive battle at Ilipa in 206 and forced the Carthaginians out of Spain.

After his Spanish victory Scipio determined to invade the Carthaginian homeland. He sailed for Africa in 204 and established a beachhead. The Carthaginian council offered terms of surrender but [reneged](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/reneged) at the last minute, pinning its hopes on one last battle. The massed Carthaginian army, led by Hannibal, was defeated at Zama. The Carthaginians accepted Scipio’s terms for peace: Carthage was forced to pay an indemnity and surrender its navy, and Spain and the Mediterranean islands were ceded to Rome.

**Second Punic War**, second (218–201 bce) in a series of wars between the [Roman Republic](https://www.britannica.com/place/Roman-Republic) and the Carthaginian (Punic) empire that resulted in Roman [hegemony](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/hegemony) over the western Mediterranean.

In the years after the [First Punic War](https://www.britannica.com/event/First-Punic-War), Rome wrested Corsica and [Sardinia](https://www.britannica.com/place/Sardinia-island-Italy) from [Carthage](https://www.britannica.com/place/Carthage-ancient-city-Tunisia) and forced Carthaginians to pay an even greater indemnity than the payment exacted immediately following the [war](https://www.britannica.com/topic/war). Eventually, however, under the leadership of [Hamilcar Barca](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Hamilcar-Barca), his son [Hannibal](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Hannibal-Carthaginian-general-247-183-BCE), and his son-in-law Hasdrubal, Carthage acquired a new base in [Spain](https://www.britannica.com/topic/history-of-Spain), whence they could renew the war against Rome.

In 219 Hannibal captured Saguntum (Sagunto) on the east coast of the [Iberian Peninsula](https://www.britannica.com/place/Iberian-Peninsula). Rome demanded his withdrawal, but Carthage refused to recall him, and Rome declared war. Because Rome controlled the sea, Hannibal led his army overland through Spain and [Gaul](https://www.britannica.com/place/Gaul-ancient-region-Europe) and across the Alps, arriving in the plain of the Po River valley in 218 bce with 20,000 [infantry](https://www.britannica.com/topic/infantry) and 6,000 [cavalry](https://www.britannica.com/topic/cavalry). Roman troops tried to bar his advance but were outmatched, and Hannibal’s hold over northern Italy was established. In 217 Hannibal, reinforced by Gallic tribesmen, marched south. Rather than attack Rome directly, he marched on [Capua](https://www.britannica.com/place/Capua-ancient-city-Italy), the second largest town in Italy, hoping to incite the populace to rebel. He won several battles but still refrained from attacking the city of Rome, even after [annihilating](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/annihilating) a huge Roman army at Cannae in 216. The defeat [galvanized](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/galvanized) Roman resistance. A brilliant defensive strategy conducted by Quintus Fabius Maximus [Cunctator](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Quintus-Fabius-Maximus-Verrucosus) harried the Carthaginians without offering battle. Thus, the two armies remained deadlocked on the Italian peninsula until 211 bce, when Rome recaptured the city of [Capua](https://www.britannica.com/place/Capua-Italy).

In 207 [Hasdrubal](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Hasdrubal-Carthaginian-general-died-207-BCE), following Hannibal’s route across the Alps, reached northern Italy with another large army supported by legions of Ligurians and Gauls. Hasdrubal marched down the peninsula to join Hannibal for an assault on Rome. Rome, exhausted by war, nevertheless raised and dispatched an army to check Hasdrubal. [Gaius Nero](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Gaius-Claudius-Nero), commander of the southern Roman army, slipped away north also and defeated Hasdrubal on the banks of the Metauros River. Hannibal maintained his position in southern Italy until 203, when he was ordered to return to Africa. Italy was free of enemy troops for the first time in 15 years. During the long mainland campaign, fighting had continued as well on Sardinia and [Sicily](https://www.britannica.com/place/Sicily), which had become Rome’s chief sources of food. Aided by internal upheaval in [Syracuse](https://www.britannica.com/place/Syracuse-Italy), Carthage reestablished its presence on the island in 215 and maintained it until 210. Meanwhile, in Spain, Roman forces maintained pressure on Carthaginian strongholds. The Roman general [Publius Scipio](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Scipio-Africanus) won a decisive battle at Ilipa in 206 and forced the Carthaginians out of Spain.

After his Spanish victory Scipio determined to invade the Carthaginian homeland. He sailed for Africa in 204 and established a beachhead. The Carthaginian council offered terms of surrender but [reneged](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/reneged) at the last minute, pinning its hopes on one last battle. The massed Carthaginian army, led by Hannibal, was defeated at Zama. The Carthaginians accepted Scipio’s terms for peace: Carthage was forced to pay an indemnity and surrender its navy, and Spain and the Mediterranean islands were ceded to Rome.
